text: A chart of accounts with several independent segments can combine into millions of possible combinations, and most would be nonsense. Cross-validation rules are what stop a user from creating most of them in the first place.

Segments are independent by default — any value in one can combine with any value in another, unless something stops it. A cross-validation rule determines whether a value in one segment can combine with specific values in another.
Every rule has two parts. A condition filter identifies which account combinations the rule applies to. A validation filter defines what's actually allowed once that condition is met.

Cross-validation combination sets are a related, simpler tool: an explicit list of valid combinations across up to five segments. Good for a finite list, but it doesn't scale as well as a pattern-based rule.

A rule can reference a value range or a hierarchy node instead of listing every value, so a new cost center added under Manufacturing is automatically covered. That completes chapter five. Chapter six puts the whole course together.
